Est-on en sécurité dans un lieu de culte: Are we safe in a place of worship?
Quatre ans après l’attentat meurtrier, t: Four years after the deadly attack, the Quebec City mosque is locked down and under surveillance.
Les horreurs qui se produisent à Jérusal: The horrors unfolding in Jerusalem and Gaza have disrupted Ramadan prayers. The day after Eid al-Fitr, the last breaking of the fast has a bitter taste for Muslims. Nearly 8,000 km away in Quebec, these atrocities are reopening old wounds.
La situation n’est pas comparable, mais: The situation is not comparable, but places of worship are often under threat. And practising one’s faith continues to be a source of fear. On Monday, April 5, 2021, a young man in a balaclava showed up in front of the Assahaba mosque, a small establishment nestled in the heart of Little Maghreb, in the Rosemont neighbourhood. Armed with an air pistol, he fired 11 shots at the walls and windows. Inside, a teacher was giving an Arabic class to 11 students. No one was hurt, but the marks of the attack are visible on the façade.
La scène a été filmée par des caméras de: The scene was captured on security cameras. “Many of those who come to the mosque are traumatized,” says Yusuf Faqiri. The day after the attack, he came to pray. That’s how he found out what had happened. “Normally, a place of worship is a place where people go to reflect and renew themselves; it’s a place of peace. So it has to be a safe place for everyone,” says Samira Laouni forcefully, standing on the sidewalk in front of the mosque at a vigil held a few days after the attack.
Une vigile discrète qui n’a attiré que q: A low-key vigil that drew only a handful of opposition politicians. Last October, five <l1>mosques</l1> were targeted in attacks within the space of a few days.
Il ne s’agit pas des seuls établissement: They are not the only places to have been vandalized. In January, swastikas were drawn on the walls of the Congregation Shaar Hashomayim synagogue in Westmount. Today, for the communities that attend them, these refuges are under threat.
Et ces attaques sont loin d’être des act: And these attacks are far from isolated. “Let’s remember the Quebec City attack. There were other assaults before January 29, 2017,” Mr. Faqiri reminds us. United in their efforts to ensure their safety, Quebec’s cultural and religious communities are demanding an end to hate crimes against places of worship.
Quatre ans après l’attentat meurtrier, t: Four years after the deadly attack, the Quebec City mosque is locked down and under surveillance. There are numerous cameras, and only people with a unique individual chip can enter the building. Thanks to fundraising and community mobilization, the mosque and its surroundings are protected. Those who watch over the centre do so as volunteers.
« Ils le font en sachant que c’est la ma: “They do it knowing that it’s the house of God and that it’s a place of tranquility,” says Mr. Benabdallah. These measures reassure the community that attends the mosque. “They can pray in peace. It lets people breathe. And the calmer we are, the more we move forward,” he continues.
« On ne veut pas vivre dans des forts re: “We don’t want to live in fortresses forever,” admits Boufeldja Benabdallah, however. A place of worship is supposed to be “open, warm and welcoming.”
Il n’y a pas que les mosquées à être tou: Mosques are not the only ones affected by hateful acts. Increasingly, religious communities are uniting in the face of these attacks. That was the case in September 2020 in Toronto. A man was killed outside a mosque in the Rexdale neighbourhood. Twenty-five civil society groups then wrote and sent a <l1>letter</l1> to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.
Ils lui demandent un plan d’action pour: They asked him for an action plan to deal with the rising number of white supremacists and neo-Nazis who attack members of minority communities in Canada. The signatories include the World Sikh Organization and the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs. The April 5 attack on the Rosemont mosque prompted the same solidarity. Rabbi Michael Whitman was at the vigil, held a few days later, to support his fellow citizens.
M. Whitman se sent particulièrement proc: Mr. Whitman feels particularly close to the issues facing the Muslim community. “Both communities are vulnerable, and the same kind of behaviour is tolerated,” he laments. For him, the April 5 attack is not to be taken lightly. Hateful acts committed against places of worship undermine people’s sense of safety, but they also reopen the feeling of rejection that these communities experience. At his synagogue in Hampstead, Mr. Whitman has also mobilized his community to prevent attacks.
Il croit avoir réussi à trouver l’équili: He believes he has managed to find a balance between security and hospitality, between a protected place and an open one. At the entrance, all bags are searched. “Even mine, to make sure no one has a weapon,” he points out. Everyone is greeted warmly, and worshippers thus feel safe practising their faith.
Le rabbin Whitman, comme Boufeldja Benab: Rabbi Whitman, like Boufeldja Benabdallah, is calling for concrete solutions to this issue. “I think we have to deal with the root of the problem. We should encourage intercultural encounters, because some people don’t necessarily feel concerned by or close to our reality,” he says. He works to raise public awareness, notably by organizing training sessions and events for young and old alike.
Une idée soutenue par la militante Samaa: It’s an idea supported by activist Samaa Elibyari, who was also at the vigil. In her view, the solution lies in inclusive political discourse and in promoting sharing. “We want a society where everyone has a place and lives in peace,” she continues in a soft but firm voice. Prejudice weighs heavily in how religious communities are perceived.
On estime que de 10 % à 30 % des actes h: An estimated 10% to 30% of hateful acts are reported to the police. Of those that are, few go to trial or result in convictions, but it is impossible to know the exact numbers, as the SPVM says it has no such data. This situation hardly encourages communities to report. “It’s extremely complicated for victims to file a complaint,” laments Denise Helly, a professor who studies hate crimes at the Institut national de la recherche scientifique (INRS).
« La loi permet difficilement aux plaint: “The law makes it hard for complaints to turn into investigations. And so victims don’t complain, and as a result the problem is underestimated. We’re going in circles,” says Ms. Helly. She sees a situation similar to that of sexual assault victims who struggle to get justice in the current system. While there are no figures on the number of attacks against places of worship, Ms. Helly notes that they are on the rise.
Un phénomène qui est loin de se limiter: It’s a phenomenon that is far from limited to Quebec: “It’s been happening in France for a long time, for example. It’s easier to attack a place of worship than a person.”
Comme pour les agressions sexuelles, il: As with sexual assault, trust between religious communities and the police has to be rebuilt. “We’re working on getting closer to communities, mainly through community police stations, which are the ones that receive the most reports,” explains Marie-Claude Dandenault, head of the Prevention and Urban Security Division of the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM). She leads the SPVM’s Hate Crimes and Hate-Motivated Incidents unit.
Une unité utile, selon Mme Helly, qui pe: It’s a useful unit, according to Ms. Helly, who believes that empathy and specialized training are needed to take complaints following hate crimes committed against places of worship. “Now we have to stop believing that the police can solve everything,” says Ms. Helly. She says the police cannot really reduce the number of hate crimes and cannot make access to justice easier. So what can be done to get there?
« Une autre solution passe par les disco: “Another solution lies in public discourse. An interfaith coalition would make things easier for communities,” she says.
Le 19 avril dernier, la Ville de Montréa: On April 19, the City of Montréal adopted a motion to strengthen the SPVM’s unit against hateful acts. Among the measures voted on is one calling for greater transparency in statistics and in the options available to victims of hate incidents and hate crimes. These are measures already in place at the Vancouver and Toronto police services.
Par contre, à en croire la communauté mu: However, according to Toronto’s Muslim community, the existence of the Toronto Police Service’s Hate Crime Unit has not improved the safety of places of worship and worshippers.
« Il y a des attaques répétées contre de: “There are repeated attacks on mosques. The police help find the perpetrators, but there is no plan to prevent it from happening,” says Fatema Abdalla, communications manager for the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM). She wants the attacks to stop and everyone to be safe. For her, the problem lies with white supremacist and far-right organizations.
<strong>Empêcher les agresseurs d’agress: Stopping aggressors from attacking (rather than helping victims protect themselves)
Louis Audet Gosselin travaille à préveni: Louis Audet Gosselin works to prevent radicalization. At the Centre for the Prevention of Radicalization Leading to Violence (CPRMV), the goal is to prevent these hateful acts and to raise awareness among police forces, but also among the general public.
« Pour ne pas laisser le fardeau de la d: “So that the burden of reporting doesn’t fall on communities alone, we’re setting up partnerships with Quebec’s Jewish and Muslim communities for joint actions,” says Mr. Audet Gosselin. It’s a way of creating dialogue, as Denise Helly recommends. But it has to go further, according to Mr. Audet Gosselin: “We need to build ties. Communities have to feel that institutions have their back.”
Et du côté des agresseurs ? « Le but est: And what about the aggressors? “The goal is to reach these people as early as possible, before they act. We offer community support for individuals who are radicalizing,” he explains. The centre also offers to help the loved ones of someone who is radicalizing.
Interrogé sur la réponse du gouvernement: Asked about the government’s response to stop hateful acts against places of worship, Benoit Charette, the minister responsible for the fight against racism, said he was concerned but remained vague. He mentioned funding for preventing radicalization and violent extremism, a project led with Geneviève Guilbault, Quebec’s public security minister, and intercultural encounters run by the Ministry of Immigration. At Public Safety Canada, the response was shorter.
La porte-parole Magali Deussing mentionn: Spokesperson Magali Deussing mentioned only the existence of <l1>financial assistance</l1> offered, among others, to places of worship to install cameras, alarm systems or fences. However, this fund is not known to everyone, and not everyone knows how to use it, explains Fo Niemi of the Centre for Research-Action on Race Relations (CRARR). For Fatema Abdalla of the NCCM in Toronto, stronger action is needed. She expects governments to condemn white supremacist groups, which are mostly to blame.
« Ils sont toujours actifs, il faut les: “They are still active, and they need to be dismantled, because they also attack other communities.”
À la vigile, les membres des différentes: At the vigil, members of the different communities were unanimous: the social harmony of all Quebecers, regardless of their faith or origins, must be protected. For them, as for Denise Helly, that means inclusive political discourse that acknowledges the systemic problems faced by Quebec’s religious and cultural communities.

‍<strong>Crime ou incident haineux, quel: ‍Hate crime or hate incident: what’s the difference?
Si on peut porter plainte à la suite d’u: While a complaint can be filed following a crime, incidents such as insults or gestures are not punishable by law.
« Une insulte peut rapidement mener à un: “An insult can quickly lead to a crime; the line is thin,” explains Marie-Claude Dandenault, head of the SPVM unit. “The incident won’t go to court, because it isn’t criminal, but we will carry out an investigation, as we would for a crime.”
Nous vous invitons à signaler les actes: We encourage you to report hateful acts, whether criminal or not, to the police by calling 911, even if you are unsure. The CPRMV takes questions, listens to accounts of hateful acts and offers support.
